feedback: If the learner justifies by pointing to the unchanged amounts, name that reasoning back as 'grouping'.
If the learner cannot say why the total is the same, return to combining the same triple two ways and comparing before asking again.
Probe with 'what's your evidence the total is still the same if you group differently?' to move from a one-off trick toward a general reason.

If a learner tries the subtraction pair, confirm (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9 — the answers differ, so subtraction cannot be regrouped the way addition can; use this only as a contrast, never as a rule to apply.
activities.intendedInsight: Grouping is a reasoning move you can justify: the total is conserved because the three quantities stay the same, no matter which pair you combine first — but this freedom holds for addition, not for subtraction.
learnerActions: Given a triple, say which two numbers you would add first.
Answer a questioner (a peer, tutor, or 'maths buddy') who asks 'Why is that allowed?' and 'Would we get the same total if we grouped the numbers differently? How do you know?'
Explain in your own words that the three amounts are unchanged, so only which pair you combine first differs.

Try a new triple such as 4+7+6 and justify which pair you would add first (here 4+6=10, then 10+7=17). Notice that 4 and 6 are not next to each other, so adding them first means changing the order as well as the grouping; the total is still 17.
Test the contrast with subtraction: work out (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, notice the answers differ, and conclude that the grouping freedom belongs to addition, not subtraction.
activities.title: Why is that allowed? Justify your grouping

feedback: For the efficient-pair item, confirm the make-ten pair and show the easy second step.
For a true/false item where a number was altered, point out that the total changed because an amount changed, not because of regrouping.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising equivalent groupings and spotting the efficient first pair is intended to consolidate that regrouping preserves the total while making the calculation easier.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would add first to make a given triple easy (e.g. for 2+8+5, which pair makes a ten?).
Judge true/false statements about whether two groupings of the same triple share a total, including an item where one number has been changed so the total genuinely differs.
activities.title: Consolidate: match, choose, and check equal totals
